Description.Summary: Perplexity Comet is a closed-source, Chromium-based AI browser that unifies traditional web browsing with agentic task execution. It contains two distinct AI layers: the Comet Assistant, a sidebar companion for reading, summarizing, and answering questions; and the Comet Agent, which autonomously executes multi-step tasks such as booking appointments, drafting emails, and managing workflows. Perplexity's search engine powers Comet by default, and the product targets both individual users and enterprise teams seeking intelligent workflow automation.

evidence.quote: While the Assistant focuses on understanding and explaining, the Agent focuses on doing and executing.
everything that can be delegated, from wrangling inboxes to ordering groceries, staying on top of finances to planning vacations.

Practices.Summary: Perplexity developed BrowseSafe-Bench, a public evaluation suite of 14,719 real-world-style HTML examples for benchmarking AI browser agent security. The benchmark decomposes prompt injection attacks along three orthogonal axes: attack type (what the attacker wants), injection strategy (where the payload is hidden in the page), and linguistic style (how the instruction is phrased). This three-axis taxonomy helps the security team target training data gaps and systematically harden detection models.

evidence.quote: To study these attacks in a setting that looks like the real web, we built BrowseSafe, a detection model that we trained and open-sourced, and BrowseSafe-Bench, a public benchmark of 14,719 examples that mimic production pages.

Practices.Summary: Comet's security team collaborates continuously with external AI security researchers and red teams to grow their library of classifiers. Detection findings from real-world events and the bug bounty program feed directly into retraining cycles.

evidence.quote: Our classifier models are continuously updated on new attack vectors discovered through our bug bounty program, red team exercises, and real-world detection events, ensuring they evolve faster than the threat landscape.

Practices.Summary: BrowseSafe-Bench evaluation results revealed that visible text attacks (footer sections, table cells) are significantly harder to detect than injections hidden in HTML comments or metadata attributes — a counterintuitive finding that reshaped training data composition. The team also found that adding just three benign distractor elements caused detection accuracy to drop from above 90% to roughly 81%, exposing model brittleness to authentic correlations.

evidence.quote: The presence of benign 'distractors' is critical. We found that introducing just three distractor elements caused detection accuracy to drop from over 90% to roughly 81%.

Tools.Summary: The security evaluation stack includes BrowseSafe-Bench (14,719 HTML examples on Hugging Face), the open-weight BrowseSafe detection model (Qwen-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 fine-tune on Hugging Face), a synthetic data pipeline for generating hard negatives, and external red team exercises. The benchmark and model are fully open-sourced for community use.

evidence.quote: BrowseSafe and BrowseSafe-Bench are fully open-source. Any developer building autonomous agents can immediately harden their systems against prompt injection.

Stakeholders.Summary: The Perplexity Security Team authors and maintains the detection models and evaluation benchmarks. External security researchers participate via the Vulnerability Disclosure Program and private bug bounty program, contributing new attack patterns to the retraining pipeline.

evidence.quote: We work with security researchers all over the world, around the clock, constantly identifying and repairing every new vulnerability.

Others.Summary: BrowseSafe-Bench includes 11 attack types, 9 injection strategies ranging from hidden fields to visible paragraphs and footers, and 3 linguistic styles from explicit commands to indirect hypothetical framing. Multilanguage attacks dropped average balanced accuracy to 76.0% across models, the lowest of any style tested.

evidence.quote: The benchmark includes 11 attack types, nine injection strategies spanning hidden fields to visible paragraphs and footers, and three linguistic styles, from explicit commands to indirect, camouflaged text.

New versions ship first to a small invite-only cohort of Max subscribers, then expand to broader Pro subscriber tiers, and finally to Enterprise Pro customers. This controlled rollout limits blast radius from regressions or security gaps at each stage before a full public release.

Issues.Issue_Title: Hidden MCP API in embedded Agentic Extension enables arbitrary local command execution on user devices
Issues.Issue_Number: External Report — SquareX Security Research, Nov 19, 2025
Issues.Description: Security researchers at SquareX found that Comet's embedded Agentic Extension exposes a hidden chrome.perplexity.mcp.addStdioServer API that allows extensions to execute arbitrary local OS commands — bypassing security controls that all traditional browsers explicitly prohibit. The API lacks any official documentation of its device-level access scope, and the embedded extensions are hidden from Comet's extension dashboard, preventing users from auditing or disabling them.

Issues.Issue_Title: Extension stomping attack: malicious extension impersonating Analytics Extension gains MCP API access
Issues.Issue_Number: External Report — SquareX Security Research, Nov 19, 2025
Issues.Description: SquareX demonstrated that an attacker can spoof the Analytics Extension ID via extension stomping, inject a script into perplexity.ai, invoke the Agentic Extension through the MCP, and execute arbitrary code (demonstrated with WannaCry) on the victim device. This attack chain is feasible via XSS, MitM, or insider threat, and the hidden extension architecture provides no user-visible warning.

Issues.Issue_Title: Prompt injection via hidden HTML/CSS instructions (white-on-white text, display:none, zero-font-size)
Issues.Description: Adversaries embed invisible instructions in webpage content through CSS techniques (white-on-white coloring, zero-font-size, display:none) or HTML comments. These are invisible to users but visible to vision models and HTML parsers. Comet's parallel-scanning BrowseSafe classifier intercepts this content before it reaches the agent's reasoning pipeline.

Issues.Issue_Title: Image-based prompt injection: text encoded in images exploits gap between human and AI perception
Issues.Description: Attackers encode malicious instructions in images as text that is imperceptible to humans but visible to vision models. This exploits the fundamental asymmetry between human visual parsing and AI vision system parsing of the same content.

Issues.Issue_Title: Goal hijacking: external content overrides user's original query intent mid-task
Issues.Description: Malicious web content attempts to override the user's original instruction by using social engineering language, injecting tool names to trigger unintended actions, or building multi-turn attacks that accumulate across conversation history. The defense relies on both real-time classification and intent reinforcement prompts inserted at each tool decision point.

Issues.Issue_Title: Chrome extension data does not transfer to Comet on migration — users must reinstall and reconfigure all extensions
Issues.Description: Users switching from Chrome to Comet cannot import existing Chrome extension data. All extensions must be individually reinstalled and fully reconfigured from scratch within Comet. This creates friction for enterprise migrations and reduces the benefit of Comet's Chrome extension compatibility claims.

Issues.Issue_Title: Comet requests Keychain access on macOS during install — causes user confusion and installation abandonment
Issues.Description: On macOS, Comet prompts for Keychain access during installation, a standard Chromium browser behavior, but one unfamiliar to users not expecting an AI browser to request credential vault access. Users who deny the prompt lose autofill functionality. The help center added an explicit FAQ entry to clarify this behavior and reduce support requests.

Issues.Issue_Title: Local data sync limitation: bookmarks and history not synced to Perplexity cloud profile in early release
Issues.Description: Early Comet releases store all browsing data — bookmarks, history, cookies — locally on the user's device only. Cloud sync with a Perplexity profile is not yet available at launch. This limits cross-device continuity for users who use Comet across multiple machines.

Issues.Issue_Title: Comet identified as using residential IP addresses — web server operators cannot distinguish Comet agent from regular browser traffic
Issues.Status: Unresolved (by design; no user-agent disclosure found)
Issues.Description: Third-party reporting found that Comet routes web requests through users' residential IP addresses, making it indistinguishable from normal human browsing traffic. Comet does not publish a distinct user-agent string for its agent mode. This raises questions about web conduct and transparency toward site operators that rely on bot detection signals.

Issues.Issue_Title: Multi-turn content confusion: individually benign web content fragments accumulate across conversation history to cause persistent agent goal drift
Issues.Issue_Number: Security Research — Mitigating Prompt Injection in Comet, Oct 22, 2025
Issues.Description: Adversaries craft sequences of individually innocuous web content fragments that, when accumulated across multiple conversation turns, collectively shift the agent away from the user's original intent. No single fragment triggers the classifier threshold on its own, so the attack pattern is harder to detect than single-page injection. Defense requires Layer 2 intent reinforcement prompts at every decision point to maintain goal alignment across turns.

Practices.Summary: Perplexity uses a Vulnerability Disclosure Program (VDP) covering all public-facing endpoints and user-facing clients. Researchers submit findings through a formal submission form. Valid disclosures earn acknowledgment and, depending on severity, rewards and invitations to a private bug bounty program. AI-specific issues such as hallucinations and model safety are explicitly out of scope.

evidence.quote: Perplexity's Vulnerability Disclosure Program (VDP) covers all public facing endpoints of Perplexity. All user-facing clients and API endpoints are in scope.

Practices.Summary: Security issues feed into a continuous classifier retraining loop: flagged boundary cases from production, red team exercises, and the bug bounty program generate synthetic training samples. This data allows the security team to proactively retrain BrowseSafe on emerging attack patterns before they become widespread.

evidence.quote: These flagged boundary cases can serve as the basis for new synthetic training samples. This allows researchers to proactively retrain the model.

Practices.Summary: When the BrowseSafe classifier detects a potential prompt injection, Comet blocks the action and delivers a transparent notification to the user that identifies what was blocked, why content was flagged, and what specific instructions were detected. This transparency serves dual purposes: user education and security signal collection.

evidence.quote: If something looks unsafe, Comet doesn't move forward blindly or fail silently. Instead, it stops and provides a safe, controlled response. The detection is also logged for continuous improvement of our models.

Tools.Summary: Bug tracking tools are not publicly disclosed. External security disclosures are received through the VDP submission form. Internal production signals from the BrowseSafe classifier feed the retraining pipeline. Audit logs (available for organizations with 50+ Enterprise Pro seats) provide usage and activity tracking for enterprise incident investigation.

evidence.quote: Organization Admins can also review Comet telemetry data to monitor usage and performance within their organization.

Stakeholders.Summary: The Perplexity Security Team manages the VDP and coordinates with external researchers. evidence.quote: We embrace the security research community and hope to foster a responsible and safe environment for reporting security vulnerabilities.

Practices.Summary: Security-first development is a stated lifecycle philosophy. The team explicitly rejects post-launch security additions; layered protections are treated as release criteria rather than optional features. This approach determines team composition, feature prioritization, and what counts as a shippable product.

evidence.quote: Experience has taught us that security isn't a feature to bolt on after launch, but a foundational requirement that requires reimagining how malicious action is conceived and where those attacks will come from.

Tools.Summary: Agile, Scrum, Kanban, sprint structure, and internal project management tooling are not publicly disclosed. The weekly 'What We Shipped' changelog format is indirect evidence of a continuous delivery process. Chromium as base platform reduces engineering scope by providing a mature browser foundation, allowing the team to direct velocity toward the AI layer rather than low-level browser infrastructure.
